profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This facility is attributed to Prime, most likely Prime Data Centers given the California and Texas registry locations. Prime Data Centers own site states the company was established in 2017 in California and is now headquartered at 400 North Ervay Street, Dallas, Texas, under founder and CEO Nicholas Laag, and describes itself as majority founder owned. The company reports 28 data centers across 13 campuses globally with a 4 plus gigawatt expansion pipeline, and lists Silicon Valley and Dallas among its confirmed North America markets, alongside Austin, Chicago, Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Sacramento, matching both states where this registry lists a Prime facility. No building specific address, opening date, or individual MW figures for this particular registry row were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
Prime Santa Clara publishes 57 MW of IT capacity across 540,000 square feet of technical space. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 57 MW supports roughly 1,425 racks; at a more conservative 10 kW per rack, a typical enterprise average, the same load supports roughly 5,700 racks. The assumption drives the result by a factor of four, and Prime publishes no rack count, so neither figure is theirs. The 540,000 square feet suggests a campus built for large footprint tenants, but density per square foot, roughly 105 W per square foot at the IT load figure, is moderate by current AI standards.

The three certifications qualify this campus for distinct workload categories. SOC 2 Type II certifies that the operator's security controls have been audited against trust service criteria over a period of time, not just at a point in time. PCI DSS certifies the facility to host payment card data environments under the card-brand compliance framework. ISO 27001 certifies that an information security management system is in place and has passed third-party audit. Together they qualify the campus for regulated financial, commercial, and security-sensitive workloads, though which tenants occupy it is not published.

Within California, this site holds the third-highest published IT capacity among facilities this site has read, out of eight that publish any megawatt figure at all, across 103 total mapped facilities in the state. It accounts for roughly 24 percent of the 242 MW of published California capacity in this site's dataset. That share reflects the scarcity of published figures as much as it reflects the campus's actual standing, because 95 of the 103 mapped California facilities publish no capacity number.
